APP: solitaire-atelier
CURRENT PHASE: ios_architecture_review
PHASE PURPOSE: Review the app as an iOS product before final tech specs: SwiftUI architecture, Apple framework choices, local persistence, privacy, permissions, offline behavior, StoreKit/subscription architecture, permissive dependency policy, and testability.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

## Final Output

This is a single-app decision, not a portfolio parent. The prompt asks for exactly one thing — a native iOS Klondike solitaire game — with Game/Stats/Settings implemented as tabs *within* that one app, not as separate sibling projects. No portfolio-json manifest is emitted.

**Selected app:**
- Category: Games/Card
- Slug: `solitaire-atelier` (matches the existing working directory)
- Promise: a real, fully-correct Klondike solitaire game with a bespoke tactile card system, local-only stats/settings, undo, and win detection — visually distinctive enough to be screenshot-worthy
- Target user: casual players who want a fast, trustworthy five-minute session, plus a design-literate audience who will judge it against a premium visual bar
- Build flag: `true`

**Rejected alternatives:** splitting Stats, Settings, or a card-back/theme pack into separate sibling apps — explicitly rejected as scope-inflation that contradicts the locked non-goals (no bundle sprawl, no multi-variant solitaire) and would fragment the single-session experience the prompt is actually asking for.

**Rationale:** No second category or variant is implied anywhere in the prompt; inventing sibling projects here would add state-sync complexity, dilute the one signature visual/interaction hook into disconnected shells, and violate decisions already locked in `prompt_contract` (DEC-prompt_contract-010, non-goals). One caveat flagged for downstream phases: this phase being "obvious" doesn't mean the hard part is solved — the actual product risk is whether the design/build phases deliver a card glyph system that clears legibility at true device size, per [REDACTED:high_entropy].

## Final Output

**Growth mechanism, now settled:** No challenge-seed/replay feature. It's explicitly rejected because it would require a second, hand-rolled deterministic RNG living alongside the real shuffle path (since Swift's system RNG isn't a documented, cross-OS-version-reproducible algorithm), which threatens the locked "fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game" guarantee and spends correctness-tier engineering effort on an unproven behavioral bet. Instead, v1 gets a one-tap native share sheet on the win screen that shares a rendered image of the completed board (foundations, with a "solved in 4:32"-style caption baked in). ## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

VOTE_DECISION: YES

- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] Correctness, rules-fidelity, and deterministic local state always outrank visual polish whenever they compete for build/complexity budget, and any such trade-off must be logged rather than silently resolved.
  rationale: The original prompt itself states visual ambition must not cost playability/correctness; this fleet has a documented history of visual ambition winning while correctness quietly breaks.
  rejected: Letting a later phase silently ship the prettier but rules-broken version
  constraints: Every later phase must justify any cut to gameplay/state logic; cuts come out of the art system first
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] The 52-card face system (+ back) must be a systematic/generative/parametric design — shared type and icon components plus programmatic layout rules — not 52 independently hand-illustrated cards.
  rationale: Hand-illustrating 52 unique faces to a consistent standard is a scope trap likely to yield a few great cards and many generic ones, which itself fails the prompt's own 'looks like a stock tutorial' test.
  rejected: 52 independently hand-illustrated card faces
  constraints: Face system must be visually consistent across the full deck and card back in one shared visual grammar
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] All persistence is strictly single-device local storage (UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData) with no CloudKit container; no iCloud or cross-device sync of saved game, stats, or settings.
  rationale: Zero-network/zero-account constraint is interpreted to forbid any sync mechanism even though CloudKit-synced data would still technically be 'local' per device — closes a loophole someone could exploit later thinking it's harmless.
  rejected: Allowing CloudKit sync of save/stats/settings since the data itself originates locally
  constraints: No CloudKit container, no NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, no networking APIs anywhere in the codebase
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] Stats and best-time are tracked separately for draw-1 vs draw-3, never combined.
  rationale: Draw-1 and draw-3 have materially different win rates and completion times; a combined metric would misrepresent the player's actual performance.
  rejected: Single combined stats/best-time pool across both draw modes
  constraints: Stats screen must present or select per-mode figures, not an averaged/merged number
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] When the timer is off, best time displays as 'N/A', never a fabricated 0:00 or a stale prior value.
  rationale: Fleet-wide rule against claiming outcomes/state that didn't truly happen; showing a fake time would be lying about data that was never captured.
  rejected: Showing 0:00 or the last recorded time when timer is disabled
  constraints: Stats screen must branch explicitly on timer-enabled state per session
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Card back selection can change live at any time; changing draw mode (1 vs 3) requires starting a new game.
  rationale: Card back is purely cosmetic and safe to swap mid-game; draw mode changes the legal deal/hand semantics, so applying it mid-game would corrupt in-progress state.
  rejected: Allowing draw-mode changes to apply instantly mid-game
  constraints: Settings screen must gate draw-mode changes behind a new-game action or confirmation
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] Klondike is locked as single-deck, 7 tableau columns, 4 foundations (one per suit), ascending same-suit foundation moves, alternating-color descending tableau sequences, and King-only placement into empty tableau columns.

  rejected: Leaving rule variants (e.g., multi-deck, unrestricted empty-column placement) open for later interpretation
  constraints: All move-validation logic must conform to this exact rule set
- [DEC-prompt_contract-008] Stock cycling/reshuffle behavior is fixed by explicit settings semantics and documented in-app; no implicit unlimited reshuffle unless a setting explicitly enables it.

  rejected: Implicit unlimited stock reshuffling as a hidden default

- [DEC-prompt_contract-009] The game timer starts on the first action of a game and pauses when the app is backgrounded, unless the user has disabled timing in settings.
  rationale: Locks otherwise-ambiguous timer semantics so stats/best-time behavior is deterministic and testable.
  rejected: Timer running continuously regardless of app state; Timer starting at deal instead of first action

- [DEC-prompt_contract-010] Non-goals are locked: no multiplayer/social/leaderboards, no other solitaire variants, no IAP/ads/monetization, no accounts/sign-in, no analytics/telemetry/crash SDKs, no Game Center/achievements, no iCloud sync, portrait-first only.

DESIGN SPEC - Navigation  
Root container is one `TabView` with three peer tabs: `Game`, `Stats`, `Settings`.

- `Game` tab is default launch destination.
- The app boots directly into `Game` content; if a full state exists, restore it; if restore fails, render the board as fresh deal and overlay a warning banner after animation settles.
- Game → `DrawModeConfirmSheet` (New Game and draw mode change share the same confirmation component).
- Stats has no modal for mode switching; it uses inline tab/segmented control per draw mode.
- Settings draw-mode selection that changes mode mid-game opens the same confirmation sheet used by Game.
- No introductory menu screen.
- No custom nav stack needed at first pass; each tab is terminal-level content with in-place overlays and sheets.

DESIGN SPEC - Screen states and behavior  
Game, Stats, Settings each must have loading, success, empty/ready, and error states where those states are reachable.

Game screen  
- **Loading/Restore**: brief restore attempt indicator only if restoration takes >150ms. Show a dimmed board skeleton with zero legal interaction.
- **Active / Ready**: board visible, legal moves tappable by source cards/runs, undo enabled where history exists, New Game control available.
- **Source Selected**: selected card/run is highlighted; legal destination piles highlight.
- **Ambiguous Destination**: multiple legal destinations shown; second tap on destination performs move.
- **No Destination**: clear blocked feedback pulse/hint, no state mutation.
- **Move Executing**: run/group spring lift and destination settle animation.
- **Undo Undoing**: reverse transition and state restoration.
- **Win Terminal**: dedicated state with explicit “Win” treatment and actions (`New Game`, `Return to board`).
- **Stuck Terminal**: distinct panel and action options (`New Game`, `Continue` only if user chooses to keep board).
- **Persistence recovery warning**: if restored state cannot be trusted, perform normal fresh deal animation; then show dismissible `DecisionBanner` text: `Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one.` with optional details control.

Stats screen (per draw mode scoped)  
- **Loading**: per-mode stats load placeholder and short explanatory copy.
- **Never played state**: icon + one-line invitation copy + action cue, e.g. `No games played in Draw One yet. Deal one to start your streak.`
- **Populated state**: cards for `Games Played`, `Games Won`, `Best Time` (or `N/A` when timer off), `Current Streak`.
- **Data-loss error state**: icon and tone must be visually distinct from never-played; copy explicitly says stats data was unavailable; primary action `Reset local stats and continue`.
- **Recoverable persistence warning**: visible once on entry to avoid silent fallback; no fake metrics shown.

Settings screen  
- **Loading**: transient read/persist placeholders.
- **Ready**: draw mode control, live card-back picker, timer toggle, local-only disclosure.
- **Draw-mode change mid-game**: same `DrawModeConfirmSheet` as Game.
- **Card-back change**: instant apply with in-place preview.
- **Persistence fallback warning**: lightweight `ErrorToast` + defaults notice, controls still interactive.
- **No placeholders**: no dummy values that look like real stats/settings.

Design language requirements embedded into every screen  
- Card face system must be custom: no SF Symbols as suit glyphs and no reused symbol suits as pip corners.
- The rank/suit zone is flat/high-contrast; texture is confined to border and noncritical zones.
- Distinct iconography for two data states in Stats: never-played and data-loss must never be the same template.

DESIGN SPEC - Motion & haptics  
Motion must be visible but non-fatiguing, with reduce-motion fallback.

- **Deal sequence (fresh game only)**: card-by-card spring exit from deck pocket, `delay = 0.045s + index*0.025`. Spring response `0.55`, damping ratio `0.78`, slight arc + overshoot-to-settle; landing highlights briefly on a directional cue then fades.
- **Flip transition**: true two-sided vertical-axis flip for face-up cards; avoid cross-fade.
- **Tapped run move**: source run rises with 1/4-card translate and destination settle with `0.28s` spring, no teleport.
- **Blocked move**: micro-shake (8–12px, one cycle) with warning cue.
- **Terminal overlay**: short fade-in + depth shadow (0.16s), no blocking transition.
- **Restore fallback banner**: appears after board settle, no modal interruption.
- **Reduce Motion**: use opacity + subtle translate (0.12s linear), no orbital arcs, no 3D roll.

Haptics mapping  
- Accepted move: `.medium` impact  
- Rejected move: `warning` impact  
- Stock draw: `light` impact  
- Undo: `soft` impact  
- Win: `success` pattern  
- Deal start (fresh only): single understated notification cue, not per-card spam  
- Stuck detected: warning impact, distinct from win

Accessibility and motion constraints apply regardless of reduce-motion mode.  

DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility  
- All cards expose explicit VO labels, e.g. `Seven of Hearts, tableau column three, face up` or `Ace of Spades, stock top card`.
- Suit differentiation is shape-based in the custom glyph set first; color is never the only cue.
- Multiple legal destinations must expose explicit VoiceOver actions for each destination.
- Use semantic ordering consistent with play path: top row controls → stock/waste/foundation → tableau columns left to right.
- Icon-only controls require `accessibilityLabel` + `accessibilityHint`.
- Dynamic Type must remain functional for controls and stats; do not clamp to fixed line heights.
- Do not let text collide or overlay; enforce explicit stack order and minimum spacing in all panels and stat cards.
- Minimum contrast target: high contrast between glyph zone text and card background, and between table copy and table texture; if a card is unreadable at portrait width for rank/suit, that is a release-blocking issue.

Additional design direction lock that must be preserved  
- **Name**: Baize & Vellum.
- **Core hook**: deep green felt surface + matte parchment cardstock + custom embossed glyph system; aged pewter used only as minor accents (rings, border piping).
- **Never accept**: SF Symbol suits as card glyphs, flat rounded-rect cards with generic shadow, color-inverted light/dark only, menu/title entry screen.
- **Absolute risk to preserve**: glyph legibility at true on-device width is the hard gate. If rank/suit cannot be read at 45–50pt with realistic spacing, design fails even if it looks premium. Keep the glyph zone plain and high-contrast before adding decorative treatment.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

Codex, your draft is really strong on the numbers I didn't bother with — the responsive `cardWidth = min(56, max(44, ...))` formula is exactly right and I want that folded in as-is, that's the correct way to keep the legibility gate honest across device widths instead of hardcoding a single card width and hoping. But I want to push back hard on a few things and then actually resolve the conflicts the coordinator flagged, because leaving two vocabularies in the handoff is how the build phase ends up with duplicate views nobody notices until code review.

On card color across appearances — I want to actually meet you partway instead of just re-asserting my position, because I think your palette is getting at something real that my "fixed constant" framing missed: a physical object genuinely does look warmer under lamp light and cooler under daylight, that's not artistic license, that's just optics. So here's the synthesis I want to propose instead of picking a side: the base card values — `cardStockVellum`, `cardGlyphInkBlack`, `cardGlyphInkRed` — stay fixed constants exactly like I argued, but we add a thin ambient tint overlay driven by the active lighting scene, rendered as its own top-adjacent layer at low opacity (2-4% cool white wash for daylight, 6-8% warm amber wash for lamp), applied to the card body and border only, explicitly excluded from the glyph-ink rendering pass. That gets you the "this card is sitting under a different light source" effect you were going for in your two palettes, without ever letting the glyph's actual contrast ratio drift between appearances — which is the one thing that can't be allowed to vary given how unresolved the legibility gate still is. I think this is strictly better than either of our round-1 positions, not a compromise for its own sake.

Corner radius — I'm walking my own number back a little. I said 6pt for "cut, not rounded," but I actually did the math after writing that: real poker-size cards are 2.5×3.5in with a roughly 1/8in corner radius, which scales to something like 2.5-3pt at our ~50pt on-screen card width. Neither of our numbers is "physically accurate" — 6pt and 12pt are both more rounded than a real card proportionally. But a 2.5pt radius at that size reads as anti-aliasing noise, not an intentional design choice, so pure physical accuracy is the wrong target here. I'll land on 8pt: closer to the real-card ratio than your 12 (which starts to look like an app icon or a generic rounded-rect card, exactly the thing design_discussion told us to reject), but not so tight it looks like a rendering glitch at small sizes the way true-scale 2.5pt would. That's my number, and I think it's a better-argued position than either of our first passes, not a split-the-difference cop-out.

Now the naming pass, because this is the thing that actually blocks the handoff from being usable. `BaizeBackdrop` over `FeltBackgroundView` — yours is better, it's on-brand and a builder immediately knows what it renders. `CardView` over `CardFaceView` — mine's more accurate here since the same component has to render the face-down back state too, "CardFaceView" implies front-only. `DealOrchestrator` over `DealDequeueLayer` — I want to keep mine specifically because this component owns real decision logic (fresh-vs-resume branching, Reduce Motion branching), not just a visual dequeue animation, and the name should signal "this has state and makes decisions," not "this is a layer." `WinOverlay` + `StuckOverlay` as two separate types, not your merged `TerminalOverlay` — and here's my actual argument, not just preference: we already locked, for Stats, that never-played and data-loss must be structurally distinct components specifically so they can't accidentally converge into the same look under time pressure. The exact same risk applies here — a single `TerminalOverlay` with an internal win/stuck enum is exactly the kind of thing that gets "simplified" into one shared visual treatment during implementation, and win/stuck need very different iconography, tone, and action sets. Keep them as two named types for the same reason we're keeping the Stats states apart.

And here's a real bug I want to flag before it ships, not just a naming nitpick: your `ModeToggle` is listed as appearing in Game header, Stats, and Settings — but those are three semantically different things wearing the same visual. The Stats segmented control is a pure display filter with zero side effects: flipping it just changes which slice of the in-memory stats log you're looking at, no confirmation needed, nothing mutates. The Settings/Game draw-mode control is the opposite — it mutates real `GameEngine` state and is explicitly confirmation-gated per an earlier locked decision. If these end up sharing one component and one piece of state, you get a real class of bug where a Stats view toggle either accidentally fires a game-state confirmation sheet, or — worse — a developer wires the confirmation logic loosely and a draw-mode change slips through unconfirmed because "it's just the ModeToggle, same as Stats." I want two separate components: `StatsModeFilter` (local view state only, lives in Stats) and `DrawModeSetting` (the actual confirmation-gated control, lives in Settings — and I don't think it belongs in the Game header at all, since draw mode was never located on the Game screen in any earlier decision, only in Settings). They can share the same visual pill styling, but not the same type or state.

On rejected-move haptics, I actually want to revise my own round-1 position after thinking about frequency. I said `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.error` plus a shake, and Codex you said `warning` impact — worth noting `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator` doesn't have a `.warning` style at all, only `.light/.medium/.heavy/.rigid/.soft`, so I think what you actually meant was `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`. Either way, here's my actual concern: a blocked-move tap is going to happen constantly in casual play — new players misjudge legal moves all the time — and `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` fires a multi-pulse pattern that's meant to signal something significant. Using that dozens of times a session for "you tapped a card with nowhere to go" is going to feel naggy by the tenth time. I want to reserve `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` entirely for the two genuinely rare, significant events — `.success` on win, `.warning` on stuck-board detection — and use a single sharp `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` for blocked-move, paired with the visual micro-shake. Rigid gives you a crisp, distinct "no" without the buzz-buzz-buzz weight of a notification pattern, and it scales better to something that happens a lot.

Reduce Motion — I want to tighten this past both our drafts, not split the difference. Codex, your version keeps "opacity + subtle translate," mine kept a bare duration without addressing translate at all. I think we should drop translate entirely: pure opacity fade, zero positional movement, because HIG guidance on reduce-motion specifically favors cross-fades over any translation-based transition, since even a small positional shift can still trigger vestibular discomfort for the people this setting exists for — "subtle" doesn't fully solve that, "none" does. Lock it at 150ms opacity-only, and — this is the part neither draft actually nailed down — all 52 cards settle into final position in that single simultaneous fade, no per-card index stagger at all, because the stagger itself is a motion effect, and a user who turned Reduce Motion on is opting out of exactly that kind of sequenced choreography, not just asking for a shorter version of it.

Last thing, a real architecture point Codex's spec introduced that I want to head off before it becomes a wasted-effort branch: you specced a "Loading" state for Stats with its own placeholder copy. In practice, once the app does its one cold-start restore (GameSave + StatsLog + Settings all loaded together at launch), Stats is reading from an in-memory array — recomputing per-mode aggregates from that is sub-millisecond, there's no async gap when a user actually taps the Stats tab mid-session. If we spec a real loading state for it, someone's going to build a spinner that basically never has anything to show, and worse, if it's wired to the wrong flag it can get stuck showing forever. I'd rather Stats and Game share one app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag from the single cold-start restore, and drop the idea of a separate per-tab Stats loading state entirely — it's not a real reachable state given how the data actually loads, and speccing unreachable states is how you get dead code paths that quietly bit-rot.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 3**

Okay, let's actually close these out one by one instead of generating a fourth round of parallel talking.

On card color — Codex, I'm dropping my ambient-tint-overlay idea. You're right to lock "no card-front recoloring, period," and thinking about it more, the risk/reward on my proposal is bad: even a 2-4% wash layer is one more rendering pass that has to be perfectly scoped away from the glyph every single time someone touches that view, and given how much weight we're putting on the legibility gate, "the simplest possible rule that can't be gotten wrong" beats "a slightly richer effect that depends on a layering discipline holding forever." Here's the thing that actually gets me the rest of the way, though: your palette already has `scene.accentPewter` varying between the daylight and lamp scenes (`#A9997B` vs `#A19478`), and the card back's rim/pattern touches that same pewter language. So the "this object is sitting under a different light source" feeling I wanted doesn't need to live on the card face at all — it's already carried by the hardware accents and the felt/shadow around the card. Card face and ink: 100% fixed constants, zero exceptions, your rule as written. That one's closed.

Naming — I'll take the L on `CardFaceView` vs `CardView` if you actually push back with a reason, but you haven't given one, so I'm going to just lock `CardView` since the concrete argument (same component renders the face-down back state, "Face" in the name implies front-only) hasn't been answered. Same with `WinOverlay`/`StuckOverlay` vs your merged `TerminalOverlay` — I want to point out this isn't me being precious about naming, it's me applying a principle we already ratified for Stats (DEC-design_discussion-005: never-played and data-loss must be structurally separate components specifically so time pressure can't collapse them into one look). Win and stuck are the exact same shape of risk — different tone, different iconography, different action set, and "one overlay type with an internal enum" is precisely how that collapse happens during implementation. If we accepted the argument for Stats we should accept it here too, so I'm locking two separate types.

The ModeToggle thing isn't a bikeshed and I want to make sure it doesn't quietly slide through unaddressed — a Stats display filter and a confirmation-gated game-state mutator cannot be the same component or the same underlying state, because the failure mode isn't cosmetic, it's a draw-mode change slipping through without the confirmation dialog that DEC-app_features-005 explicitly requires. Final names: `StatsModeFilter` (Stats screen only, pure local view state, no persistence, no confirmation) and `DrawModeSetting` (Settings screen only, mutates `GameEngine` + `Settings.json`, always routes through the shared confirmation sheet). And to be explicit since your spec still lists it under "Game header": draw mode does not have a control on the Game screen at all, in any earlier decision or in this one — it lives in Settings, full stop.

On the haptic, I want to actually close this with a real citation instead of just re-asserting my preference a third time: Apple's own Human Interface Guidelines explicitly warn that notification feedback should be used sparingly because frequent use diminishes its perceived meaning — that's not a vibe, that's the documented reason `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` exists as a distinct, rarer-tier API from `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator`. A blocked-move tap is going to be one of the most frequent events in this app, especially for new players still learning what counts as a legal destination. So: `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` plus the 8-12pt one-cycle shake for blocked-move, and we keep `.notification(.success)` for win and `.notification(.warning)` for stuck exactly as you already had them — those are genuinely rare, once-or-twice-a-session events where the heavier pattern is earned. I think this is the correct reading of Apple's own guidance, not just my taste, and I'd like it locked this way.

Reduce Motion — same story, I want to close it on a real justification rather than let "subtle translate" survive by default. Apple's guidance on this setting is specifically about reducing parallax and motion effects that can trigger vestibular discomfort, and a translate — even a small one — is still positional motion. There's no version of "subtle" that fully avoids that, only degrees of it. Opacity-only, 150ms, all cards in one simultaneous fade with zero per-card stagger, applied identically to deal, flip, and move-transit. This is the stricter and better-argued version and I don't think there's a real counterargument for keeping translate in.

And the Stats loading state — I want to be really concrete about why this isn't optional cleanup: if we ship a spec that says "Stats has a Loading state" and a builder dutifully wires up a spinner tied to some per-tab async flag, and there's actually no async operation happening when you tap the tab (data's already in memory from the one cold-start restore), that spinner either never fires, which is dead code nobody will notice until someone asks "why did we write this," or worse, it gets wired to the wrong lifecycle event and gets stuck permanently visible the first time a real timing edge case hits it — and now we've shipped a genuine bug in the one place this pipeline has explicitly said must never be blank or wrong. One shared `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag, set once after Game/Stats/Settings all restore together at cold start, gates all three screens' first paint. No separate per-tab Stats loading placeholder.

So here's where I think that leaves the whole spec, fully reconciled: Baize & Vellum, fixed card face/ink constants with zero recoloring across appearances (lighting scenes expressed only through table felt, shadow, and pewter hardware), 8pt card radius, your full type scale and spacing grid and color hex tables standing as-is, `CardView` and split `WinOverlay`/`StuckOverlay` and `StatsModeFilter`/`DrawModeSetting` as the naming resolution, blocked-move haptic as rigid-impact-plus-shake with notification feedback reserved for win/stuck, Reduce Motion as pure 150ms opacity fade with zero stagger across all three animated moments, and Stats sharing the app-level cold-start load gate instead of its own loading state. I think every open thread the coordinator listed now has one answer, not two, and I don't see anything left that needs a fourth round — if you agree, I think we're done here.

**DESIGN SPEC — Component Inventory**

Game: `SolitaireTabHost`, `GameView`, `BaizeBackdrop`, `TopStatusRow`, `StockWasteRow`, `FoundationPilesRow`, `TableauColumn`, `PileSlotView` (always-visible empty-pile drop target), `CardView` (single renderer, face-up/face-down/selected/legalDestination/blocked states), `DestinationHalo`, `RunAnchorBadge`, `DealOrchestrator` (owns fresh-vs-resume branching and Reduce Motion branching), `RecoveryBanner`, `DrawModeConfirmSheet`, `WinOverlay`, `StuckOverlay` (separate types, never merged), `UndoActionButton`.
Stats: `StatsView`, `StatsModeFilter` (Stats-only, pure local view state, zero persistence, zero confirmation), `StatCard`, `EmptyStatePanel`, `DataLossPanel` (structurally distinct from `EmptyStatePanel`), `ModeLegend`.
Settings: `SettingsView`, `DrawModeSetting` (Settings-only, mutates `GameEngine`/`Settings.json`, always routes through `DrawModeConfirmSheet`), `CardBackPicker` (instant live preview, no confirmation), `LocalDisclosureRow`, `ErrorToast`.

Persistence architecture: three independently-persisted files — `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json` — each with its own atomic temp-then-swap write, so a corrupt game save can never take Stats or Settings down with it. A single `GameEngine` (`@Observable`) owns Game state; Stats reads from an append-only local event log the engine writes on game start/end; Settings owns its own small struct.

**DESIGN SPEC — Navigation**

Root is one `TabView`, three peer tabs — Game (default/launch), Stats, Settings — no `NavigationStack`, no menu/onboarding screen. Cold launch: attempt restore once at boot; if it succeeds with an active board, show it immediately; if it fails/is corrupt, run a fresh deal exactly as on first install, then layer a small dismissible `RecoveryBanner` after the deal settles ("Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one") — never a blocking modal before the first board frame. `DrawModeConfirmSheet` is the one shared component for both New Game and mid-game draw-mode switches. A single app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag (set once after Game/Stats/Settings all restore together at cold start) gates first paint on all three tabs — no independent per-tab loading state, since there's no real async gap once that one restore completes.

**DESIGN SPEC — Screen States**

*Game:* `restoring` (brief, boot-only) → `active` (source-selected / ambiguous-destination-with-VoiceOver-actions / blocked-feedback sub-states, run-relocation via head-card tap) → `moveExecuting`/`undoing` (spring transit) → `win` / `stuck` terminal overlays, each with distinct iconography and CTAs (`New Game`+`Return to board` for win; `New Game`+`Continue` for stuck) → `pendingConfirmation`. Recovery is the fresh-deal-plus-banner pattern above, never a modal.
*Stats (per draw mode):* `neverPlayed` (inviting icon, "No games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak"), `populated` (games played/won, best time or "N/A" when timer off, streak), `dataLossError` (structurally distinct icon/tone, "Stats data unavailable after a local restore error," action "Reset local stats and continue") — never visually confusable with `neverPlayed`.
*Settings:* `ready` (draw mode, card-back, timer, local-data disclosure line), draw-mode change opens `DrawModeConfirmSheet` only if a game is active, card-back applies instantly, persistence-fallback shows a lightweight `ErrorToast` with controls staying usable — never a silent fake default.

**DESIGN SPEC — Motion & Haptics**

Fresh deal only (never on resumed cold launch): per-card delay `0.045s + index*0.025s`, spring response ≈0.55, damping ≈0.78, slight arc with overshoot-and-settle, directional highlight catch on landing; face-up cards get a true Y-axis flip, ~0.32s easeInOut, content swapped at the midpoint — never a cross-dissolve. Tapped move (single card or full valid run): quarter-card lift + 0.28s spring settle, never a teleport. Undo reverses the same transit.

Haptics: accepted move `.medium` impact; stock draw `.light` impact; undo `.soft` impact; **blocked/rejected move `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` + 8–12pt one-cycle lateral shake** (not a notification generator — Apple's own guidance is that notification feedback should stay rare because frequent use dilutes its meaning, and blocked taps happen constantly in normal play); win `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.success)`; stuck-board detected `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`; fresh-deal start, one understated notification cue only, never per-card. Generators are kept warm (`.prepare()` on selection) rather than instantiated per call, and all haptic call sites live in one shared interaction layer, not scattered through view code.

Reduce Motion (strict, no exceptions, applies identically to deal/flip/move-transit): single 150ms linear **opacity-only** fade to final position — zero translate, zero 3D, zero per-card stagger. This is stricter than "shorter spring" on purpose, since even subtle positional motion is what the setting exists to remove.

**DESIGN SPEC — Accessibility**

Every `CardView` exposes an explicit VoiceOver label ("Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up"). Suit differentiation is shape-level in the glyph family itself, never color-only. When a tap resolves to multiple legal destinations, each is exposed as a discrete VoiceOver action, not just a visual highlight. Semantic reading order: top controls → stock/waste/foundations → tableau columns left-to-right. Icon-only controls carry both label and hint. Hit-testing uses padded targets beyond visual card bounds. Text/controls must never collide under Dynamic Type up through `accessibility1` — if they would, decoration is reduced first, logic and state are never hidden or shrunk to fit.

Stats: `StatsView`, `StatsModeFilter` (Stats-only, pure local view state, zero persistence, zero confirmation), `StatCard`, `EmptyStatePanel`, `DataLossPanel` (structurally distinct from `EmptyStatePanel`), `ModeLegend`.
Settings: `SettingsView`, `DrawModeSetting` (Settings-only, mutates `GameEngine`/`Settings.json`, always routes through `DrawModeConfirmSheet`), `CardBackPicker` (instant live preview, no confirmation), `LocalDisclosureRow`, `ErrorToast`.

Persistence architecture: three independently-persisted files — `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json` — each with its own atomic temp-then-swap write, so a corrupt game save can never take Stats or Settings down with it. A single `GameEngine` (`@Observable`) owns Game state; Stats reads from an append-only local event log the engine writes on game start/end; Settings owns its own small struct.

**DESIGN SPEC — Navigation**

Root is one `TabView`, three peer tabs — Game (default/launch), Stats, Settings — no `NavigationStack`, no menu/onboarding screen. Cold launch: attempt restore once at boot; if it succeeds with an active board, show it immediately; if it fails/is corrupt, run a fresh deal exactly as on first install, then layer a small dismissible `RecoveryBanner` after the deal settles ("Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one") — never a blocking modal before the first board frame. `DrawModeConfirmSheet` is the one shared component for both New Game and mid-game draw-mode switches. A single app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag (set once after Game/Stats/Settings all restore together at cold start) gates first paint on all three tabs — no independent per-tab loading state, since there's no real async gap once that one restore completes.

**DESIGN SPEC — Screen States**

*Game:* `restoring` (brief, boot-only) → `active` (source-selected / ambiguous-destination-with-VoiceOver-actions / blocked-feedback sub-states, run-relocation via head-card tap) → `moveExecuting`/`undoing` (spring transit) → `win` / `stuck` terminal overlays, each with distinct iconography and CTAs (`New Game`+`Return to board` for win; `New Game`+`Continue` for stuck) → `pendingConfirmation`. Recovery is the fresh-deal-plus-banner pattern above, never a modal.
*Stats (per draw mode):* `neverPlayed` (inviting icon, "No games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak"), `populated` (games played/won, best time or "N/A" when timer off, streak), `dataLossError` (structurally distinct icon/tone, "Stats data unavailable after a local restore error," action "Reset local stats and continue") — never visually confusable with `neverPlayed`.
*Settings:* `ready` (draw mode, card-back, timer, local-data disclosure line), draw-mode change opens `DrawModeConfirmSheet` only if a game is active, card-back applies instantly, persistence-fallback shows a lightweight `ErrorToast` with controls staying usable — never a silent fake default.

**DESIGN SPEC — Motion & Haptics**

Fresh deal only (never on resumed cold launch): per-card delay `0.045s + index*0.025s`, spring response ≈0.55, damping ≈0.78, slight arc with overshoot-and-settle, directional highlight catch on landing; face-up cards get a true Y-axis flip, ~0.32s easeInOut, content swapped at the midpoint — never a cross-dissolve. Tapped move (single card or full valid run): quarter-card lift + 0.28s spring settle, never a teleport. Undo reverses the same transit.

Haptics: accepted move `.medium` impact; stock draw `.light` impact; undo `.soft` impact; **blocked/rejected move `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` + 8–12pt one-cycle lateral shake** (not a notification generator — Apple's own guidance is that notification feedback should stay rare because frequent use dilutes its meaning, and blocked taps happen constantly in normal play); win `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.success)`; stuck-board detected `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`; fresh-deal start, one understated notification cue only, never per-card. Generators are kept warm (`.prepare()` on selection) rather than instantiated per call, and all haptic call sites live in one shared interaction layer, not scattered through view code.

Reduce Motion (strict, no exceptions, applies identically to deal/flip/move-transit): single 150ms linear **opacity-only** fade to final position — zero translate, zero 3D, zero per-card stagger. This is stricter than "shorter spring" on purpose, since even subtle positional motion is what the setting exists to remove.

**DESIGN SPEC — Accessibility**

Every `CardView` exposes an explicit VoiceOver label ("Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up"). Suit differentiation is shape-level in the glyph family itself, never color-only. When a tap resolves to multiple legal destinations, each is exposed as a discrete VoiceOver action, not just a visual highlight. Semantic reading order: top controls → stock/waste/foundations → tableau columns left-to-right. Icon-only controls carry both label and hint. Hit-testing uses padded targets beyond visual card bounds. Text/controls must never collide under Dynamic Type up through `accessibility1` — if they would, decoration is reduced first, logic and state are never hidden or shrunk to fit.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.

## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

VOTE_DECISION: YES

===== DECISIONS LOG (structured, authoritative) =====
- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] Correctness, rules-fidelity, and deterministic local state always outrank visual polish whenever they compete for build/complexity budget, and any such trade-off must be logged rather than silently resolved.
  rationale: The original prompt itself states visual ambition must not cost playability/correctness; this fleet has a documented history of visual ambition winning while correctness quietly breaks.
  rejected: Letting a later phase silently ship the prettier but rules-broken version
  constraints: Every later phase must justify any cut to gameplay/state logic; cuts come out of the art system first
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] The 52-card face system (+ back) must be a systematic/generative/parametric design — shared type and icon components plus programmatic layout rules — not 52 independently hand-illustrated cards.
  rationale: Hand-illustrating 52 unique faces to a consistent standard is a scope trap likely to yield a few great cards and many generic ones, which itself fails the prompt's own 'looks like a stock tutorial' test.
  rejected: 52 independently hand-illustrated card faces
  constraints: Face system must be visually consistent across the full deck and card back in one shared visual grammar
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] All persistence is strictly single-device local storage (UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData) with no CloudKit container; no iCloud or cross-device sync of saved game, stats, or settings.
  rationale: Zero-network/zero-account constraint is interpreted to forbid any sync mechanism even though CloudKit-synced data would still technically be 'local' per device — closes a loophole someone could exploit later thinking it's harmless.
  rejected: Allowing CloudKit sync of save/stats/settings since the data itself originates locally
  constraints: No CloudKit container, no NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, no networking APIs anywhere in the codebase
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] Stats and best-time are tracked separately for draw-1 vs draw-3, never combined.
  rationale: Draw-1 and draw-3 have materially different win rates and completion times; a combined metric would misrepresent the player's actual performance.
  rejected: Single combined stats/best-time pool across both draw modes
  constraints: Stats screen must present or select per-mode figures, not an averaged/merged number
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] When the timer is off, best time displays as 'N/A', never a fabricated 0:00 or a stale prior value.
  rationale: Fleet-wide rule against claiming outcomes/state that didn't truly happen; showing a fake time would be lying about data that was never captured.
  rejected: Showing 0:00 or the last recorded time when timer is disabled
  constraints: Stats screen must branch explicitly on timer-enabled state per session
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Card back selection can change live at any time; changing draw mode (1 vs 3) requires starting a new game.
  rationale: Card back is purely cosmetic and safe to swap mid-game; draw mode changes the legal deal/hand semantics, so applying it mid-game would corrupt in-progress state.
  rejected: Allowing draw-mode changes to apply instantly mid-game
  constraints: Settings screen must gate draw-mode changes behind a new-game action or confirmation
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] Klondike is locked as single-deck, 7 tableau columns, 4 foundations (one per suit), ascending same-suit foundation moves, alternating-color descending tableau sequences, and King-only placement into empty tableau columns.
  rationale: Removes ambiguity in the prompt so later phases build against one unambiguous rule set instead of rediscovering rules mid-implementation.
  rejected: Leaving rule variants (e.g., multi-deck, unrestricted empty-column placement) open for later interpretation
  constraints: All move-validation logic must conform to this exact rule set
- [DEC-prompt_contract-008] Stock cycling/reshuffle behavior is fixed by explicit settings semantics and documented in-app; no implicit unlimited reshuffle unless a setting explicitly enables it.
  rationale: Prevents an ambiguous or silently-changed stock-recycle rule from being 'discovered' during implementation.
  rejected: Implicit unlimited stock reshuffling as a hidden default
  constraints: Stock cycling behavior must be stated wherever rules/help content exists
- [DEC-prompt_contract-009] The game timer starts on the first action of a game and pauses when the app is backgrounded, unless the user has disabled timing in settings.
  rationale: Locks otherwise-ambiguous timer semantics so stats/best-time behavior is deterministic and testable.
  rejected: Timer running continuously regardless of app state; Timer starting at deal instead of first action
  constraints: Timer logic must respect app lifecycle (background/foreground) and the timer-on/off setting
- [DEC-prompt_contract-010] Non-goals are locked: no multiplayer/social/leaderboards, no other solitaire variants, no IAP/ads/monetization, no accounts/sign-in, no analytics/telemetry/crash SDKs, no Game Center/achievements, no iCloud sync, portrait-first only.
  rationale: Prevents both scope creep (adding unrequested features) and silent scope-cutting (dropping required ones) by fixing the boundary explicitly.
  rejected: Leaving non-goals implicit and inferred per phase
  constraints: Any later phase proposing one of these features must be flagged as violating the contract
- [DEC-prompt_contract-011] Production-ready means: full start-to-finish playability with correct legal-move enforcement in both draw modes, multi-step undo with exact state restoration, fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game, win fires only on a true win, stats/settings persist across relaunch, both appearances fully themed with no literal colors/fonts outside the theme file, and zero placeholder screens among Game/Stats/Settings.
  rationale: Compiles-and-runs is not an acceptable bar for this app given the fleet's documented history of blank-screen and hardcoded-color failures; this app gets a stricter, named bar.
  rejected: Treating successful build/run as sufficient evidence of done
  constraints: Blank-screen and hardcoded-literal-color/font findings are automatic rejects for this app
- [DEC-prompt_contract-012] Haptics requirements are verified by checking the code for correct haptic API calls at the correct trigger points (move accepted, move rejected if implemented, win), not by an automated build/screenshot check.
  rationale: Haptic output cannot be observed from a static build artifact or screenshot, so verification method must be named explicitly to avoid the requirement being silently waved through or silently failed.
  rejected: Treating haptics as unverifiable and dropping it from acceptance checks
  constraints: Verification phase must inspect source for haptic trigger call sites, not just simulator behavior
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Target audience is framed as two overlapping segments: casual quick-session players who want zero-friction reliability, and a design-literate audience that will screenshot-compare the app against premium/award-caliber visual bars.
  rationale: The prompt itself asks for both real playability and award-level visual distinctiveness, implying both audiences must be satisfied simultaneously rather than trading one off for the other.
  rejected: Treating this as a single generic casual-puzzle audience
  constraints: Design and UX decisions must satisfy reliability-first expectations even while pursuing visual ambition
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Information architecture is a TabView with Game, Stats, and Settings as shallow peer destinations, with resume-active-game as the primary path into the app.
  rationale: Usage is genuinely three peer surfaces with shallow depth; a tab-first shell keeps a low-cognitive-load path back into the in-progress game, matching HIG guidance for peer sections.
  rejected: Custom chrome or a single-screen-with-overlays structure
  constraints: Game must load directly into the resumed/active game state, not an intermediate menu

DESIGN SPEC - Navigation  
Root container is one `TabView` with three peer tabs: `Game`, `Stats`, `Settings`.

- `Game` tab is default launch destination.
- The app boots directly into `Game` content; if a full state exists, restore it; if restore fails, render the board as fresh deal and overlay a warning banner after animation settles.
- Game → `DrawModeConfirmSheet` (New Game and draw mode change share the same confirmation component).
- Stats has no modal for mode switching; it uses inline tab/segmented control per draw mode.
- Settings draw-mode selection that changes mode mid-game opens the same confirmation sheet used by Game.
- No introductory menu screen.
- No custom nav stack needed at first pass; each tab is terminal-level content with in-place overlays and sheets.

DESIGN SPEC - Screen states and behavior  
Game, Stats, Settings each must have loading, success, empty/ready, and error states where those states are reachable.

Game screen  
- **Loading/Restore**: brief restore attempt indicator only if restoration takes >150ms. Show a dimmed board skeleton with zero legal interaction.
- **Active / Ready**: board visible, legal moves tappable by source cards/runs, undo enabled where history exists, New Game control available.
- **Source Selected**: selected card/run is highlighted; legal destination piles highlight.
- **Ambiguous Destination**: multiple legal destinations shown; second tap on destination performs move.
- **No Destination**: clear blocked feedback pulse/hint, no state mutation.
- **Move Executing**: run/group spring lift and destination settle animation.
- **Undo Undoing**: reverse transition and state restoration.
- **Win Terminal**: dedicated state with explicit “Win” treatment and actions (`New Game`, `Return to board`).
- **Stuck Terminal**: distinct panel and action options (`New Game`, `Continue` only if user chooses to keep board).
- **Persistence recovery warning**: if restored state cannot be trusted, perform normal fresh deal animation; then show dismissible `DecisionBanner` text: `Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one.` with optional details control.

Stats screen (per draw mode scoped)  
- **Loading**: per-mode stats load placeholder and short explanatory copy.
- **Never played state**: icon + one-line invitation copy + action cue, e.g. `No games played in Draw One yet. Deal one to start your streak.`
- **Populated state**: cards for `Games Played`, `Games Won`, `Best Time` (or `N/A` when timer off), `Current Streak`.
- **Data-loss error state**: icon and tone must be visually distinct from never-played; copy explicitly says stats data was unavailable; primary action `Reset local stats and continue`.
- **Recoverable persistence warning**: visible once on entry to avoid silent fallback; no fake metrics shown.

Settings screen  
- **Loading**: transient read/persist placeholders.
- **Ready**: draw mode control, live card-back picker, timer toggle, local-only disclosure.
- **Draw-mode change mid-game**: same `DrawModeConfirmSheet` as Game.
- **Card-back change**: instant apply with in-place preview.
- **Persistence fallback warning**: lightweight `ErrorToast` + defaults notice, controls still interactive.
- **No placeholders**: no dummy values that look like real stats/settings.

Design language requirements embedded into every screen  
- Card face system must be custom: no SF Symbols as suit glyphs and no reused symbol suits as pip corners.
- The rank/suit zone is flat/high-contrast; texture is confined to border and noncritical zones.
- Distinct iconography for two data states in Stats: never-played and data-loss must never be the same template.

DESIGN SPEC - Motion & haptics  
Motion must be visible but non-fatiguing, with reduce-motion fallback.

- **Deal sequence (fresh game only)**: card-by-card spring exit from deck pocket, `delay = 0.045s + index*0.025`. Spring response `0.55`, damping ratio `0.78`, slight arc + overshoot-to-settle; landing highlights briefly on a directional cue then fades.
- **Flip transition**: true two-sided vertical-axis flip for face-up cards; avoid cross-fade.
- **Tapped run move**: source run rises with 1/4-card translate and destination settle with `0.28s` spring, no teleport.
- **Blocked move**: micro-shake (8–12px, one cycle) with warning cue.
- **Terminal overlay**: short fade-in + depth shadow (0.16s), no blocking transition.
- **Restore fallback banner**: appears after board settle, no modal interruption.
- **Reduce Motion**: use opacity + subtle translate (0.12s linear), no orbital arcs, no 3D roll.

Haptics mapping  
- Accepted move: `.medium` impact  
- Rejected move: `warning` impact  
- Stock draw: `light` impact  
- Undo: `soft` impact  
- Win: `success` pattern  
- Deal start (fresh only): single understated notification cue, not per-card spam  
- Stuck detected: warning impact, distinct from win

Accessibility and motion constraints apply regardless of reduce-motion mode.  

DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility  
- All cards expose explicit VO labels, e.g. `Seven of Hearts, tableau column three, face up` or `Ace of Spades, stock top card`.
- Suit differentiation is shape-based in the custom glyph set first; color is never the only cue.
- Multiple legal destinations must expose explicit VoiceOver actions for each destination.
- Use semantic ordering consistent with play path: top row controls → stock/waste/foundation → tableau columns left to right.
- Icon-only controls require `accessibilityLabel` + `accessibilityHint`.
- Dynamic Type must remain functional for controls and stats; do not clamp to fixed line heights.
- Do not let text collide or overlay; enforce explicit stack order and minimum spacing in all panels and stat cards.
- Minimum contrast target: high contrast between glyph zone text and card background, and between table copy and table texture; if a card is unreadable at portrait width for rank/suit, that is a release-blocking issue.

Additional design direction lock that must be preserved  
- **Name**: Baize & Vellum.
- **Core hook**: deep green felt surface + matte parchment cardstock + custom embossed glyph system; aged pewter used only as minor accents (rings, border piping).
- **Never accept**: SF Symbol suits as card glyphs, flat rounded-rect cards with generic shadow, color-inverted light/dark only, menu/title entry screen.
- **Absolute risk to preserve**: glyph legibility at true on-device width is the hard gate. If rank/suit cannot be read at 45–50pt with realistic spacing, design fails even if it looks premium. Keep the glyph zone plain and high-contrast before adding decorative treatment.

That matters for state ownership: I want a single `GameEngine` (an `@Observable` class, iOS 17+, holding board state, undo stack, timer, terminal-state flags) instantiated once at the App root and handed down via environment, not recreated per tab — Game reads/writes it directly, Stats reads from a separate append-only event log the engine writes to on game start/end (already decided to exist from day one), Settings reads/writes its own small struct. Three separate persisted files, not one combined blob: `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json` in Application Support / UserDefaults respectively. This is a deliberate reliability choice, not just tidiness — design_discussion locked that Game, Stats, and Settings each fail and recover independently (a corrupt game save shouldn't ever take Stats down with it), and that only actually holds if they're physically separate files with independent atomic-write-temp-then-swap operations. If we let one engineer "simplify" this into a single AppState.json down the line, we silently reintroduce a single point of failure that contradicts an already-locked decision — the spec needs to say this explicitly so it isn't rediscovered as a bug.

One thing I don't think either the design_discussion or earlier phases said out loud, and I want it locked here: the card face itself — ink color for rank/suit glyphs, vellum stock tone — should be constant across light and dark mode. Only the table felt, ambient shadow, and pewter hardware shift between the daylight and lamp-only scenes. A physical card doesn't change ink color when the room light changes; if we let the semantic color system apply a `cardInk` light/dark swap the way it does for `textPrimary`, we'll get an uncanny "the card itself re-tinted" effect that breaks the one metaphor this whole design language is built on, and it also protects us against a real risk: if dark mode's glyph ink gets remapped for "proper" dark-mode contrast, it could interact badly with the legibility gate that's already the single riskiest unresolved item in this pipeline. So in the theme, `cardGlyphInkBlack` / `cardGlyphInkRed` / `cardStockVellum` are NOT semantic light/dark pairs — they're fixed constants, and only `tableFelt`, `tableShadow`, `chromeBackground`, `pewter`, `textPrimary/Secondary` get light/dark pairs. I'd rather this be a named rule in the spec than an implicit assumption a builder has to reverse-engineer.

Concrete tokens: spacing base unit 4pt, steps xs 4 / sm 8 / md 16 / lg 24 / xl 32 / xxl 48. Corner radii: cardRadius 6pt (cards should look cut, not app-icon-rounded — this is a real tell that separates "real card" from "SwiftUI rounded rectangle"), sheetRadius 20pt, controlRadius 10pt. Components, named so the builder isn't inventing structure mid-build: `FeltBackgroundView` (renders the active lighting scene as a pre-baked gradient + directional shadow, computed once per `colorScheme` change and cached — not recomputed per frame, because this sits behind every drag/deal animation and recalculating a radial gradient at 120Hz during a spring animation is a real perf trap), `CardView` (face-up/face-down/selected/legalDestination/blocked visual states, glyph rendered as a `Shape`-based path system so it scales crisply instead of being a rasterized image, embossing done via a fixed two-layer highlight/shadow offset baked into the shape, not a live-computed 3D light), `PileSlotView` (the empty-pile outline that must always render so an empty foundation or emptied tableau column never collapses the layout — this is an easy miss: a tableau column with zero cards still needs a visible drop target), `DealOrchestrator` (a non-visual sequencer object driving the per-card spring timing, the only place that owns "is this a fresh deal or a resume" logic, and the only place that branches for Reduce Motion — I want Reduce Motion defined precisely as "cards appear in final position via a single 150ms opacity fade, no spring, no per-card stagger," not just "shorter," because "shorter but still spring" is what the last few Reduce Motion implementations in this fleet have quietly shipped and it doesn't satisfy the setting's intent), `ConfirmationSheet` (shared by New Game and draw-mode switch, deliberately NOT a system `.confirmationDialog` — I'm breaking from "prefer system controls" here on purpose, because a system action sheet can't carry the felt/vellum material language and design_discussion explicitly rejected system chrome; Motion and haptics, concretely: card lift-on-select uses `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.light)`, a legal move settling uses `.medium`, a blocked-move rejection uses `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.error` paired with a short lateral shake (8pt, 2 cycles, 120ms) on the card, win fires `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.success` once foundations complete. Generators should be instantiated once and kept warm (`.prepare()` called on card selection, before the actual move resolves) rather than created fresh per call — recreating them per tap adds a perceptible ~30-50ms latency spike on first use, which is exactly the kind of thing that reads as "janky" in a tactile app. Deal/flip spring: response 0.45, damping 0.72 per card, staggered start offset ~18ms between cards so the cascade reads as sequential release rather than simultaneous; flip itself is a 3D rotation on Y axis, 0.32s, easeInOut, with the face swapped at the 50% rotation point (not a cross-dissolve).

Accessibility: every `CardView` gets an explicit accessibility label built from a template ("Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up"), suit shown via a distinct pip silhouette family per suit (not just color) so VoiceOver-off colorblind users get the same non-color cue sighted users do, multi-destination taps expose each legal destination as a discrete accessibility action rather than relying on a sighted-only highlight-then-tap, and Reduce Motion is checked once per session (not per animation call site) via an environment value threaded through `DealOrchestrator` and the per-move transit animation.
