**Codex (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 2**

I’m not going to paper over the round1 split: we should lock the visual spec in one place now, and I’m endorsing Claude’s point on fixed card ink plus a tighter card silhouette because that directly protects the 45–50pt legibility gate more than any “premium” tweak. Codex, your palette discipline is strong, but when we make card color a light/dark pair, we risk the one thing this spec already calls out as a hard failure—indistinguishable or fuzzy glyphs under edge lighting. So for this handoff, card ink/stock tone is constant across both appearances, and only table, shadow, and pewter hardware are scene-specific. I also think Claude is right on rejectability: 12pt corners look app-icon-rounded; we need a flatter, real-card geometry, so I’m locking card radius at 8 and keep the foundation/tableau slots cleaner at 10. For motion feedback, we’ll keep rejected-move haptics as `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` error for a clearer, less ambiguous signal than a “warning” impact.

Type scale is locked to `Theme.Fonts`: Display 1 34 semibold mapped to `.largeTitle`, Display 2 28 semibold mapped to `.title`, Heading 1 24 semibold `.title2`, Heading 2 20 medium `.title3`, Body 17 regular `.body`, Body Emphasis 17 semibold `.body`, Callout 16 medium `.callout`, Caption 13 medium `.caption`, Micro 12 regular `.footnote`, Small 10.5 regular `.caption2`; card typography is separate and custom via vector glyph rendering, with Rank 24 semibold, Suit 18 regular, Center motif 14 regular, and optional back micro-mark 10 medium from `Theme.Fonts.caption`. I’m also keeping a concrete sizing rule for board geometry: `cardWidth = min(56, max(44, (contentWidth - (6*cardStackHorizontalGap + 2*boardSideInset))/7))` with `cardAspectRatio = 1.57`, and this must stay true so readability is tested at true 7-column width, not a blown-up preview.

Spacing grid is base 4 and is explicit everywhere: xxs 4, xs 8, sm 12, md 16, lg 20, xl 24, xxl 32, xxxl 40, maxInset 16, boardSideInset 16, boardTopInset 12, boardBottomInset 10, cardStackHorizontalGap 6, componentGap 14, cardRunLabelGap 6. For card stack geometry, runVerticalOffsetFaceDown is 10, runVerticalOffsetFaceUp is 16, tableauColumns is 7, tableauCardLiftHitPadding is 10, foundationStackGap is 0, topRowHeightFactor is 1.0, statusRowHeight is 44. Nothing can drift from those without an explicit change.

Color semantics are two lighting scenes with one shared card system. Light scene (Daylight Through Window): `scene.background #F0E7D0`, `scene.surfaceBase #1B583E`, `scene.surfaceWash #2C7B52`, `scene.surfaceDepth #103A27`, `scene.vignette #081F14`, `scene.accentPewter #A9997B`, `text.primary #F8F5EC`, `text.secondary #D5D2C4`, `text.disabled #B3AE9F`, `success #2F9A64`, `warning #D0892A`, `error #C64848`, `focusRing #F3E4C2`, ambient highlight `#F0E0B0`. Dark scene (Lamp-Only Night): `scene.background #0F2F25`, `scene.surfaceBase #194A36`, `scene.surfaceWash #1C5A3F`, `scene.surfaceDepth #0A271D`, `scene.vignette #060F0C`, `scene.accentPewter #A19478`, `text.primary #EDE2CB`, `text.secondary #C3B89F`, `text.disabled #AFA89B`, `success #48B57C`, `warning #E8A64E`, `error #E57575`, `focusRing #DCC89B`, ambient highlight `#8A6E47`. Card constants are fixed across modes by design: `card.frontBase #F6ECD2`, `card.frontPaper #F9F2DB`, `card.frontEdge #D7C9A7`, `card.frontShadow #BFAF8D`, `card.backBase #D1B68C`, `card.backRim #A78A63`, `card.backPattern #C4A57A`, `card.inkBlack #2A2214`, `card.inkRed #8A2A22`, `card.onCard #2A2214`. No card-front semantic recoloring in dark mode. If this gets challenged during implementation, we are violating the locked anti-casino/anti-gimmick direction and the legibility gate.

Corner radii are named and fixed: `radius.card` 8, `radius.pile` 10, `radius.panel` 18, `radius.toast` 14, `radius.button` 12, `radius.modal` 22. Cards are not pill-shaped and not app-icon rounded; this is a deliberate realism cue.

Interaction model keeps the existing engine contract and does not invent extra complexity: single `TabView` at root with three peer tabs: Game, Stats, Settings. No menu screen, no `NavigationStack` needed first pass, no hierarchy beyond tabs and overlays. The app starts in Game, attempts restore on launch, and if restore is clean and active, jumps into board directly; if restore fails, it must still play a fresh deal and then show a dismissible non-blocking recovery banner. Shared confirmation component is mandatory for any New Game and any draw-mode change while game is active.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

Codex, your draft is really strong on the numbers I didn't bother with — the responsive `cardWidth = min(56, max(44, ...))` formula is exactly right and I want that folded in as-is, that's the correct way to keep the legibility gate honest across device widths instead of hardcoding a single card width and hoping. On card color across appearances — I want to actually meet you partway instead of just re-asserting my position, because I think your palette is getting at something real that my "fixed constant" framing missed: a physical object genuinely does look warmer under lamp light and cooler under daylight, that's not artistic license, that's just optics. So here's the synthesis I want to propose instead of picking a side: the base card values — `cardStockVellum`, `cardGlyphInkBlack`, `cardGlyphInkRed` — stay fixed constants exactly like I argued, but we add a thin ambient tint overlay driven by the active lighting scene, rendered as its own top-adjacent layer at low opacity (2-4% cool white wash for daylight, 6-8% warm amber wash for lamp), applied to the card body and border only, explicitly excluded from the glyph-ink rendering pass. That gets you the "this card is sitting under a different light source" effect you were going for in your two palettes, without ever letting the glyph's actual contrast ratio drift between appearances — which is the one thing that can't be allowed to vary given how unresolved the legibility gate still is. I think this is strictly better than either of our round-1 positions, not a compromise for its own sake.

Corner radius — I'm walking my own number back a little. I said 6pt for "cut, not rounded," but I actually did the math after writing that: real poker-size cards are 2.5×3.5in with a roughly 1/8in corner radius, which scales to something like 2.5-3pt at our ~50pt on-screen card width. Neither of our numbers is "physically accurate" — 6pt and 12pt are both more rounded than a real card proportionally. But a 2.5pt radius at that size reads as anti-aliasing noise, not an intentional design choice, so pure physical accuracy is the wrong target here. I'll land on 8pt: closer to the real-card ratio than your 12 (which starts to look like an app icon or a generic rounded-rect card, exactly the thing design_discussion told us to reject), but not so tight it looks like a rendering glitch at small sizes the way true-scale 2.5pt would. That's my number, and I think it's a better-argued position than either of our first passes, not a split-the-difference cop-out.

Now the naming pass, because this is the thing that actually blocks the handoff from being usable. `BaizeBackdrop` over `FeltBackgroundView` — yours is better, it's on-brand and a builder immediately knows what it renders. `CardView` over `CardFaceView` — mine's more accurate here since the same component has to render the face-down back state too, "CardFaceView" implies front-only. `DealOrchestrator` over `DealDequeueLayer` — I want to keep mine specifically because this component owns real decision logic (fresh-vs-resume branching, Reduce Motion branching), not just a visual dequeue animation, and the name should signal "this has state and makes decisions," not "this is a layer." `WinOverlay` + `StuckOverlay` as two separate types, not your merged `TerminalOverlay` — and here's my actual argument, not just preference: we already locked, for Stats, that never-played and data-loss must be structurally distinct components specifically so they can't accidentally converge into the same look under time pressure. The exact same risk applies here — a single `TerminalOverlay` with an internal win/stuck enum is exactly the kind of thing that gets "simplified" into one shared visual treatment during implementation, and win/stuck need very different iconography, tone, and action sets. Keep them as two named types for the same reason we're keeping the Stats states apart.

And here's a real bug I want to flag before it ships, not just a naming nitpick: your `ModeToggle` is listed as appearing in Game header, Stats, and Settings — but those are three semantically different things wearing the same visual. The Stats segmented control is a pure display filter with zero side effects: flipping it just changes which slice of the in-memory stats log you're looking at, no confirmation needed, nothing mutates. The Settings/Game draw-mode control is the opposite — it mutates real `GameEngine` state and is explicitly confirmation-gated per an earlier locked decision. If these end up sharing one component and one piece of state, you get a real class of bug where a Stats view toggle either accidentally fires a game-state confirmation sheet, or — worse — a developer wires the confirmation logic loosely and a draw-mode change slips through unconfirmed because "it's just the ModeToggle, same as Stats." I want two separate components: `StatsModeFilter` (local view state only, lives in Stats) and `DrawModeSetting` (the actual confirmation-gated control, lives in Settings — and I don't think it belongs in the Game header at all, since draw mode was never located on the Game screen in any earlier decision, only in Settings). They can share the same visual pill styling, but not the same type or state.

On rejected-move haptics, I actually want to revise my own round-1 position after thinking about frequency. I said `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.error` plus a shake, and Codex you said `warning` impact — worth noting `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator` doesn't have a `.warning` style at all, only `.light/.medium/.heavy/.rigid/.soft`, so I think what you actually meant was `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`. Either way, here's my actual concern: a blocked-move tap is going to happen constantly in casual play — new players misjudge legal moves all the time — and `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` fires a multi-pulse pattern that's meant to signal something significant. Using that dozens of times a session for "you tapped a card with nowhere to go" is going to feel naggy by the tenth time. I want to reserve `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` entirely for the two genuinely rare, significant events — `.success` on win, `.warning` on stuck-board detection — and use a single sharp `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` for blocked-move, paired with the visual micro-shake. Rigid gives you a crisp, distinct "no" without the buzz-buzz-buzz weight of a notification pattern, and it scales better to something that happens a lot.

Reduce Motion — I want to tighten this past both our drafts, not split the difference. Codex, your version keeps "opacity + subtle translate," mine kept a bare duration without addressing translate at all. I think we should drop translate entirely: pure opacity fade, zero positional movement, because HIG guidance on reduce-motion specifically favors cross-fades over any translation-based transition, since even a small positional shift can still trigger vestibular discomfort for the people this setting exists for — "subtle" doesn't fully solve that, "none" does. Lock it at 150ms opacity-only, and — this is the part neither draft actually nailed down — all 52 cards settle into final position in that single simultaneous fade, no per-card index stagger at all, because the stagger itself is a motion effect, and a user who turned Reduce Motion on is opting out of exactly that kind of sequenced choreography, not just asking for a shorter version of it.

Last thing, a real architecture point Codex's spec introduced that I want to head off before it becomes a wasted-effort branch: you specced a "Loading" state for Stats with its own placeholder copy. In practice, once the app does its one cold-start restore (GameSave + StatsLog + Settings all loaded together at launch), Stats is reading from an in-memory array — recomputing per-mode aggregates from that is sub-millisecond, there's no async gap when a user actually taps the Stats tab mid-session. If we spec a real loading state for it, someone's going to build a spinner that basically never has anything to show, and worse, if it's wired to the wrong flag it can get stuck showing forever. I'd rather Stats and Game share one app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag from the single cold-start restore, and drop the idea of a separate per-tab Stats loading state entirely — it's not a real reachable state given how the data actually loads, and speccing unreachable states is how you get dead code paths that quietly bit-rot.

Win and stuck are the exact same shape of risk — different tone, different iconography, different action set, and "one overlay type with an internal enum" is precisely how that collapse happens during implementation. If we accepted the argument for Stats we should accept it here too, so I'm locking two separate types.

The ModeToggle thing isn't a bikeshed and I want to make sure it doesn't quietly slide through unaddressed — a Stats display filter and a confirmation-gated game-state mutator cannot be the same component or the same underlying state, because the failure mode isn't cosmetic, it's a draw-mode change slipping through without the confirmation dialog that DEC-app_features-005 explicitly requires. Final names: `StatsModeFilter` (Stats screen only, pure local view state, no persistence, no confirmation) and `DrawModeSetting` (Settings screen only, mutates `GameEngine` + `Settings.json`, always routes through the shared confirmation sheet). And to be explicit since your spec still lists it under "Game header": draw mode does not have a control on the Game screen at all, in any earlier decision or in this one — it lives in Settings, full stop.

On the haptic, I want to actually close this with a real citation instead of just re-asserting my preference a third time: Apple's own Human Interface Guidelines explicitly warn that notification feedback should be used sparingly because frequent use diminishes its perceived meaning — that's not a vibe, that's the documented reason `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` exists as a distinct, rarer-tier API from `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator`. A blocked-move tap is going to be one of the most frequent events in this app, especially for new players still learning what counts as a legal destination. So: `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` plus the 8-12pt one-cycle shake for blocked-move, and we keep `.notification(.success)` for win and `.notification(.warning)` for stuck exactly as you already had them — those are genuinely rare, once-or-twice-a-session events where the heavier pattern is earned. I think this is the correct reading of Apple's own guidance, not just my taste, and I'd like it locked this way.

Reduce Motion — same story, I want to close it on a real justification rather than let "subtle translate" survive by default. Apple's guidance on this setting is specifically about reducing parallax and motion effects that can trigger vestibular discomfort, and a translate — even a small one — is still positional motion. There's no version of "subtle" that fully avoids that, only degrees of it. Opacity-only, 150ms, all cards in one simultaneous fade with zero per-card stagger, applied identically to deal, flip, and move-transit. This is the stricter and better-argued version and I don't think there's a real counterargument for keeping translate in.

And the Stats loading state — I want to be really concrete about why this isn't optional cleanup: if we ship a spec that says "Stats has a Loading state" and a builder dutifully wires up a spinner tied to some per-tab async flag, and there's actually no async operation happening when you tap the tab (data's already in memory from the one cold-start restore), that spinner either never fires, which is dead code nobody will notice until someone asks "why did we write this," or worse, it gets wired to the wrong lifecycle event and gets stuck permanently visible the first time a real timing edge case hits it — and now we've shipped a genuine bug in the one place this pipeline has explicitly said must never be blank or wrong. One shared `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag, set once after Game/Stats/Settings all restore together at cold start, gates all three screens' first paint. No separate per-tab Stats loading placeholder.

So here's where I think that leaves the whole spec, fully reconciled: Baize & Vellum, fixed card face/ink constants with zero recoloring across appearances (lighting scenes expressed only through table felt, shadow, and pewter hardware), 8pt card radius, your full type scale and spacing grid and color hex tables standing as-is, `CardView` and split `WinOverlay`/`StuckOverlay` and `StatsModeFilter`/`DrawModeSetting` as the naming resolution, blocked-move haptic as rigid-impact-plus-shake with notification feedback reserved for win/stuck, Reduce Motion as pure 150ms opacity fade with zero stagger across all three animated moments, and Stats sharing the app-level cold-start load gate instead of its own loading state. I think every open thread the coordinator listed now has one answer, not two, and I don't see anything left that needs a fourth round — if you agree, I think we're done here.

## Final Output

**Design language:** Baize & Vellum, carried forward unchanged from design_discussion — deep green felt table, matte parchment card stock with embossed bespoke glyphs, aged pewter as small hardware accents only, two art-directed lighting scenes (daylight-through-window / lamp-only-at-night), signature per-card staggered spring deal + true two-sided flip on fresh deals only.

**DESIGN SPEC — Type Scale** (all via `Theme.Fonts`, mapped to Dynamic Type, zero inline font literals in views)

| Role | Size (pt) | Weight | Dynamic Type style |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Display 1 | 34 | Semibold | `.largeTitle` |
| Display 2 | 28 | Semibold | `.title` |
| Heading 1 | 24 | Semibold | `.title2` |
| Heading 2 | 20 | Medium | `.title3` |

Card typography (custom vector glyph system, not system fonts): Rank 24pt semibold, Suit 18pt regular, Center motif 14pt regular, back micro-mark 10pt medium (`Theme.Fonts.caption` weight family). Must stay legible at true tableau card width (44–56pt, see formula below) up through Dynamic Type `accessibility1` — this is the hard release gate; if it fails, strip decoration before touching layout logic.

**DESIGN SPEC — Spacing Grid** (base unit 4pt)

xxs 4, xs 8, sm 12, md 16, lg 20, xl 24, xxl 32, xxxl 40. Layout constants: `boardSideInset` 16, `boardTopInset` 12, `boardBottomInset` 10, `maxInset` 16, `cardStackHorizontalGap` 6, `componentGap` 14, `cardRunLabelGap` 6, `statusRowHeight` 44, `foundationStackGap` 0, `topRowHeightFactor` 1.0, `runVerticalOffsetFaceDown` 10, `runVerticalOffsetFaceUp` 16, `tableauColumns` 7, `tableauCardLiftHitPadding` 10.

Card sizing: `cardWidth = min(56, max(44, (contentWidth - (6*cardStackHorizontalGap + 2*boardSideInset)) / 7))`, `cardAspectRatio = 1.57`. This formula, not a fixed width, is what keeps the legibility gate honest across device sizes.

**DESIGN SPEC — Semantic Color Palette**

Light scene (Daylight Through Window): `scene.background #F0E7D0`, `scene.surfaceBase #1B583E`, `scene.surfaceWash #2C7B52`, `scene.surfaceDepth #103A27`, `scene.vignette #081F14`, `scene.ambientHighlight #F0E0B0`, `text.primary #F8F5EC`, `text.secondary #D5D2C4`, `text.disabled #B3AE9F`, `scene.pewter #A9997B`, `success #2F9A64`, `warning #D0892A`, `error #C64848`, `focusRing #F3E4C2`.

Dark scene (Lamp-Only Night): `scene.background #0F2F25`, `scene.surfaceBase #194A36`, `scene.surfaceWash #1C5A3F`, `scene.surfaceDepth #0A271D`, `scene.vignette #060F0C`, `scene.ambientHighlight #8A6E47`, `text.primary #EDE2CB`, `text.secondary #C3B89F`, `text.disabled #AFA89B`, `scene.pewter #A19478`, `success #48B57C`, `warning #E8A64E`, `error #E57575`, `focusRing #DCC89B`.

Card system constants — **fixed, scene-agnostic, zero light/dark variation, zero ambient wash of any kind**: `card.frontBase #F6ECD2`, `card.frontPaper #F9F2DB`, `card.frontEdge #D7C9A7`, `card.frontShadow #BFAF8D`, `card.backBase #D1B68C`, `card.backRim #A78A63`, `card.backPattern #C4A57A`, `card.inkBlack #2A2214`, `card.inkRed #8A2A22`, `card.onCard #2A2214`. The "different light source" feeling is carried entirely by `scene.pewter`, table felt, and ambient shadow — never by recoloring the card itself.

**DESIGN SPEC — Corner Radii**: `radius.card` 8, `radius.pile` 10, `radius.panel` 18, `radius.toast` 14, `radius.button` 12, `radius.modal` 22. Cards are deliberately not pill-shaped or app-icon-rounded.

**DESIGN SPEC — Component Inventory**

Game: `SolitaireTabHost`, `GameView`, `BaizeBackdrop`, `TopStatusRow`, `StockWasteRow`, `FoundationPilesRow`, `TableauColumn`, `PileSlotView` (always-visible empty-pile drop target), `CardView` (single renderer, face-up/face-down/selected/legalDestination/blocked states), `DestinationHalo`, `RunAnchorBadge`, `DealOrchestrator` (owns fresh-vs-resume branching and Reduce Motion branching), `RecoveryBanner`, `DrawModeConfirmSheet`, `WinOverlay`, `StuckOverlay` (separate types, never merged), `UndoActionButton`.
Stats: `StatsView`, `StatsModeFilter` (Stats-only, pure local view state, zero persistence, zero confirmation), `StatCard`, `EmptyStatePanel`, `DataLossPanel` (structurally distinct from `EmptyStatePanel`), `ModeLegend`.
Settings: `SettingsView`, `DrawModeSetting` (Settings-only, mutates `GameEngine`/`Settings.json`, always routes through `DrawModeConfirmSheet`), `CardBackPicker` (instant live preview, no confirmation), `LocalDisclosureRow`, `ErrorToast`.

Persistence architecture: three independently-persisted files — `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json` — each with its own atomic temp-then-swap write, so a corrupt game save can never take Stats or Settings down with it. A single `GameEngine` (`@Observable`) owns Game state; Stats reads from an append-only local event log the engine writes on game start/end; Settings owns its own small struct.

**DESIGN SPEC — Navigation**

Root is one `TabView`, three peer tabs — Game (default/launch), Stats, Settings — no `NavigationStack`, no menu/onboarding screen. Cold launch: attempt restore once at boot; if it succeeds with an active board, show it immediately; if it fails/is corrupt, run a fresh deal exactly as on first install, then layer a small dismissible `RecoveryBanner` after the deal settles ("Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one") — never a blocking modal before the first board frame. `DrawModeConfirmSheet` is the one shared component for both New Game and mid-game draw-mode switches. A single app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag (set once after Game/Stats/Settings all restore together at cold start) gates first paint on all three tabs — no independent per-tab loading state, since there's no real async gap once that one restore completes.

**DESIGN SPEC — Screen States**

*Game:* `restoring` (brief, boot-only) → `active` (source-selected / ambiguous-destination-with-VoiceOver-actions / blocked-feedback sub-states, run-relocation via head-card tap) → `moveExecuting`/`undoing` (spring transit) → `win` / `stuck` terminal overlays, each with distinct iconography and CTAs (`New Game`+`Return to board` for win; `New Game`+`Continue` for stuck) → `pendingConfirmation`. Recovery is the fresh-deal-plus-banner pattern above, never a modal.
*Stats (per draw mode):* `neverPlayed` (inviting icon, "No games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak"), `populated` (games played/won, best time or "N/A" when timer off, streak), `dataLossError` (structurally distinct icon/tone, "Stats data unavailable after a local restore error," action "Reset local stats and continue") — never visually confusable with `neverPlayed`.
*Settings:* `ready` (draw mode, card-back, timer, local-data disclosure line), draw-mode change opens `DrawModeConfirmSheet` only if a game is active, card-back applies instantly, persistence-fallback shows a lightweight `ErrorToast` with controls staying usable — never a silent fake default.

**DESIGN SPEC — Motion & Haptics**

Fresh deal only (never on resumed cold launch): per-card delay `0.045s + index*0.025s`, spring response ≈0.55, damping ≈0.78, slight arc with overshoot-and-settle, directional highlight catch on landing; face-up cards get a true Y-axis flip, ~0.32s easeInOut, content swapped at the midpoint — never a cross-dissolve. Tapped move (single card or full valid run): quarter-card lift + 0.28s spring settle, never a teleport. Undo reverses the same transit.

Haptics: accepted move `.medium` impact; stock draw `.light` impact; undo `.soft` impact; **blocked/rejected move `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` + 8–12pt one-cycle lateral shake** (not a notification generator — Apple's own guidance is that notification feedback should stay rare because frequent use dilutes its meaning, and blocked taps happen constantly in normal play); win `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.success)`; stuck-board detected `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`; fresh-deal start, one understated notification cue only, never per-card. Generators are kept warm (`.prepare()` on selection) rather than instantiated per call, and all haptic call sites live in one shared interaction layer, not scattered through view code.

Reduce Motion (strict, no exceptions, applies identically to deal/flip/move-transit): single 150ms linear **opacity-only** fade to final position — zero translate, zero 3D, zero per-card stagger. This is stricter than "shorter spring" on purpose, since even subtle positional motion is what the setting exists to remove.

**DESIGN SPEC — Accessibility**

Every `CardView` exposes an explicit VoiceOver label ("Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up"). Suit differentiation is shape-level in the glyph family itself, never color-only. When a tap resolves to multiple legal destinations, each is exposed as a discrete VoiceOver action, not just a visual highlight. Semantic reading order: top controls → stock/waste/foundations → tableau columns left-to-right. Icon-only controls carry both label and hint. Hit-testing uses padded targets beyond visual card bounds. Text/controls must never collide under Dynamic Type up through `accessibility1` — if they would, decoration is reduced first, logic and state are never hidden or shrunk to fit.

**Must / Should / Could / Won't** (restated per Codex's earlier quality-gate request)
- **Must:** Game/Stats/Settings triad, resume-first launch, draw-1/draw-3 parity, full legal-move + run-relocation + undo path, both terminal states, Theme-only styling with zero hardcoded literals, full accessibility labeling/actions, honest non-blocking persistence-failure states everywhere.
- **Should:** run one real on-device legibility pass at true card width before the glyph shapes are considered locked in code; enforce the `cardWidth` formula in every layout path, never a fixed constant.
- **Could:** further micro-tuning of felt/shadow/pewter lighting fidelity once gameplay correctness and the legibility gate are both confirmed.
- **Won't:** win-screen share sheet, live interactive drag, third-party frameworks/packages, any encrypted local persistence layer, any card-face recoloring or ambient wash tied to appearance.

**No external Claude Design pass is required** — every numeric value a SwiftUI builder needs (fonts, spacing, colors, radii, component names, states, motion curves, haptic call sites) is pinned above with zero adjectives standing in for numbers. **DESIGN SPEC — Navigation**

Root is one `TabView`, three peer tabs — Game (default/launch), Stats, Settings — no `NavigationStack`, no menu/onboarding screen. **DESIGN SPEC — Screen States**

*Game:* `restoring` (brief, boot-only) → `active` (source-selected / ambiguous-destination-with-VoiceOver-actions / blocked-feedback sub-states, run-relocation via head-card tap) → `moveExecuting`/`undoing` (spring transit) → `win` / `stuck` terminal overlays, each with distinct iconography and CTAs (`New Game`+`Return to board` for win; `New Game`+`Continue` for stuck) → `pendingConfirmation`. **DESIGN SPEC — Motion & Haptics**

Fresh deal only (never on resumed cold launch): per-card delay `0.045s + index*0.025s`, spring response ≈0.55, damping ≈0.78, slight arc with overshoot-and-settle, directional highlight catch on landing; face-up cards get a true Y-axis flip, ~0.32s easeInOut, content swapped at the midpoint — never a cross-dissolve. Tapped move (single card or full valid run): quarter-card lift + 0.28s spring settle, never a teleport. Undo reverses the same transit.

Haptics: accepted move `.medium` impact; stock draw `.light` impact; undo `.soft` impact; **blocked/rejected move `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` + 8–12pt one-cycle lateral shake** (not a notification generator — Apple's own guidance is that notification feedback should stay rare because frequent use dilutes its meaning, and blocked taps happen constantly in normal play); win `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.success)`; stuck-board detected `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`; fresh-deal start, one understated notification cue only, never per-card. Generators are kept warm (`.prepare()` on selection) rather than instantiated per call, and all haptic call sites live in one shared interaction layer, not scattered through view code.

Reduce Motion (strict, no exceptions, applies identically to deal/flip/move-transit): single 150ms linear **opacity-only** fade to final position — zero translate, zero 3D, zero per-card stagger. This is stricter than "shorter spring" on purpose, since even subtle positional motion is what the setting exists to remove.

**DESIGN SPEC — Accessibility**

Every `CardView` exposes an explicit VoiceOver label ("Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up"). Suit differentiation is shape-level in the glyph family itself, never color-only. When a tap resolves to multiple legal destinations, each is exposed as a discrete VoiceOver action, not just a visual highlight. Semantic reading order: top controls → stock/waste/foundations → tableau columns left-to-right. Icon-only controls carry both label and hint. Hit-testing uses padded targets beyond visual card bounds. Text/controls must never collide under Dynamic Type up through `accessibility1` — if they would, decoration is reduced first, logic and state are never hidden or shrunk to fit.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.

I’d lock the architecture as a pure local, SwiftUI-first app with a thin domain core and strict state ownership: a single `@Observable` `GameEngine` that owns canonical Klondike logic and a live board state, plus separate `StatsLogStore` and `SettingsStore` services that are restored and persisted independently. That gives you the required three-screen separation (Game/Stats/Settings) without hidden state coupling and prevents a bad game save from breaking stats/settings recovery.

For framework choice, stay strictly on Apple frameworks only: SwiftUI for all screens and overlays, Foundation for Codable models and file I/O, Observation for reactivity, `DispatchQueue`/`Task` for async disk work, and UIKit haptics (`UIImpactFeedbackGenerator`, `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator`) for tactile events. No networking frameworks are needed for this build; avoid URLSession entirely. `SwiftData` is unnecessary given the locked three-file persistence contract; `Codable` + `FileManager` in Application Support is the cleanest and most testable fit here. Keep the file path abstraction behind a protocol so persistence can be tested with temp directories.

The persistence model should be exactly three independent persisted artifacts: `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json`, each with its own version stamp and atomic write path (`encode -> temp file -> flush -> atomic replace`). This is not just a design choice; it is the reliability boundary: one corrupt file must not block the others. Persist only logical game state and never transient animation offsets. Ensure every restore path is explicit and classified into success, fallback/default, and data-loss states so the UI can show the non-blocking recovery banner instead of pretending old state was valid.

For state shape, define pure value-model types (no UI types in model) with deterministic move rules and replayable undo metadata; this is the testability anchor. `GameState` should be serializable as compact, versioned JSON. Save points should be event-driven (startup, game mutation that settles state, explicit end-of-game, settings updates, timer start/stop) and include minimal metadata for compatibility/migration checks. Add a compact schema field in each file so corrupted or older data can be replaced cleanly.

Offline behavior should be explicit in the architecture: no network calls, no sign-in, no backend adapters, no sync jobs, no background fetch, no push, and no silent server fallback. Use `scenePhase` and app lifecycle hooks only to pause/resume timer state as already decided. When restoring, do one cold-boot pass only; once loaded, the app should be fully functional with airplane mode or offline launch and keep full playability. Privacy/perms surface should be minimal and stable: there are no user-data collection permissions required, no photos/camera/microphone/location/trackable IDs needed, and no background modes.
